李白: Li Bai was a romantic poet of the High Tang period, known as the 'Immortal Poet', whose poetry was bold and unrestrained, rich in imagination, and he was paired with Du Fu as 'Li Du'.
杜甫: Du Fu was a realist poet of the High Tang period, known as the 'Sage Poet', whose extensive poetic content was called 'Poetic History', and he was paired with Li Bai as 'Li Du'.
王维: Wang Wei was a famous poet, painter, and musician of the High Tang period, known as the representative of 'poetry in painting, painting in poetry'.
孟浩然: Meng Haoran was from Xiangyang during the High Tang period, known for his landscape and pastoral poetry, with a clear, distant, and uniquely transcendental poetic style.
白居易: Bai Juyi was a realist poet of the Mid-Tang Dynasty, whose poetry was approachable and widely circulated, known as 'Yuan Bai' or 'Liu Bai'.
王昌龄: Wang Changling was a famous frontier poet of the High Tang, whose poems were clear and elegant in emotion, and he was as famous as Gao Shi and Wang Zhihuan, known as 'Wang Jiangning'.
杜牧: Du Mu was from Jingzhao Wannian during the late Tang Dynasty, known as 'Xiao Du', whose poetic style was bold and elegant, and he was paired with Li Shangyin as 'Xiao Li Du'.
李商隐: Li Shangyin was a famous poet of the late Tang Dynasty, whose poetry was ornate and emotionally complex, especially known for his love poems and untitled poems.
柳宗元: Liu Zongyuan was a famous literary figure of the Tang Dynasty who advocated for the Old Prose Movement; his essays were profound and elegant, and his poetry was also very well-known.
刘禹锡: Liu Yuxi was a Tang Dynasty poet and philosopher who was once exiled. His poetry style was bold and unconstrained, and he and Bai Juyi were collectively known as "Liu Bai."
张继: Zhang Ji, courtesy name Yisun, was a Tang Dynasty poet and a successful candidate in the imperial examination during the Tianbao era. His poetry style was elegant and refined, and he is particularly famous for "Mooring by Maple Bridge at Night."
王之涣: Wang Zhihuan was a famous poet of the Tang Dynasty. His poems were grand and majestic, with his frontier poetry being particularly outstanding, and his representative work is "Climbing the Stork Tower."
孟郊: Meng Jiao, courtesy name Dongye, was a Tang Dynasty poet and a close friend of Han Yu. He passed the imperial examination late in life and was known for his strange and obscure poetic style and painstaking dedication.
贾岛: Jia Dao, courtesy name Langxian, was a Tang Dynasty poet who was once a monk. He is associated with the idiom "tuiqiao" (deliberating) due to his painstaking efforts in refining poetic lines, and his poetic style was unique, strange, and austere.
苏轼: Su Shi was from Meishan during the Northern Song Dynasty, a Northern Song literary figure and calligrapher, together with his father Su Xun and brother Su Zhe known as 'Three Sus', and his lyrical style was bold and unrestrained.
辛弃疾: Xin Qiji was from Jinan during the Southern Song Dynasty, a representative of the Haofang (bold and unconstrained) school of lyricists, paired with Su Shi as 'Su Xin', and his lyrics were passionate and inspiring.
李清照: Li Qingzhao was a famous female lyricist of the Song Dynasty, pseudonym Yi'an Jushi, who pioneered a unique Wanyue (graceful and subtle) style, with representative works such as 'Postface to Records on Metal and Stone'.
柳永: Liu Yong was from Chong'an during the Northern Song Dynasty, skilled in composing lyrics, and a representative of the Wanyue (graceful and subtle) school of lyricists.
岳飞: Yue Fei, courtesy name Pengju, was a famous general who resisted the Jin during the Southern Song Dynasty. He was loyal to his country and achieved great military successes, but was later framed and killed by the treacherous minister Qin Hui, leaving behind powerful works like "Man Jiang Hong."
陆游: Lu You was a poet and historian of the Southern Song Dynasty, who lived to be 85 years old. He advocated for resisting the Jin and recovering lost territories, was a famous patriotic poet, and was known as "Fangweng."
范仲淹: Fan Zhongyan, courtesy name Xiwen, was a statesman and literary figure of the Northern Song Dynasty. He presided over the "Qingli New Policies" and was famous for his philosophy of "being concerned before the world's worries and enjoying after the world's joys."
欧阳修: Ouyang Xiu was a literary figure and historian of the Northern Song Dynasty, one of the Eight Masters of Tang and Song Dynasties, who experienced ups and downs in officialdom throughout his life, and was famous for his literary reforms and historical works.
晏殊: Yan Shu was a famous ci poet of the Northern Song Dynasty. As a child prodigy, he rose to the position of prime minister, and his ci poetry is known for its graceful and ornate style, earning him the title of "Prime Minister Poet."
秦观: Qin Guan was a ci poet of the Northern Song Dynasty, renowned alongside Su Shi and Huang Tingjian. He was a representative figure of the graceful and restrained (wanyue) school, with his ci poetry known for its delicate emotions, and he was known as "Master Huaihai."
姜夔: Jiang Kui was a famous lyricist of the Southern Song Dynasty, courtesy name Yaozhang, pseudonym Baishi Daoren, whose poetry formed its own school, with a clear and refined style, and he was proficient in musical theory.
周邦彦: Zhou Bangyan was a famous lyricist of the late Northern Song Dynasty, courtesy name Meicheng, pseudonym Qingzhen Jushi, proficient in musical theory, and a representative of the metrical ci school of the Song Dynasty.
佚名: This is a collection of classical poems by unknown authors, selected from anthologies such as 'Classic of Poetry,' 'Complete Tang Poems,' and 'Song Ci'.
曹操: Cao Cao was a famous statesman, military strategist, and literary figure in the late Eastern Han Dynasty; he used poetry to reflect the suffering of the people and express his political ambitions.
李煜: Li Yu was the last monarch of the Southern Tang Dynasty, whose lyrical style was mournful and lingering, a famous lyricist of the late Southern Tang, with representative works such as 'Yu Meiren'.
温庭筠: Wen Tingyun was a poet and lyricist of the late Tang Dynasty, known for his outstanding poetic and lyrical talent, and was as famous as Li Shangyin, together called 'Wen Li'.
韦庄: Wei Zhuang was a poet and ci writer of the late Tang and Five Dynasties period. His poetry and ci were elegant and refined, and he was a representative writer of the Huajian (Flower Garland) ci school.
马致远: Ma Zhiyuan was a Yuan Dynasty Chinese playwright and sanqu writer; this collection includes 50 of his poems.
张养浩: Zhang Yanghao was a Yuan Dynasty sanqu writer; this collection includes 22 of his works.
徐再思: Xu Zaisi was a Yuan Dynasty sanqu writer; this collection includes 16 of his works.
宋方壶: Yuan Dynasty sanqu writer. This collection includes 19 pieces.
张可久: Zhang Kejiu was a Yuan Dynasty sanqu writer; this collection includes 50 of his works.
纳兰性德: Nalan Xingde was a famous lyricist in the early Qing Dynasty, born into a prominent family, whose lyrics were sincere and subtle, unique in style, and he died at the young age of thirty-one.
王建: Wang Jian was a Mid-Tang Dynasty poet, skilled in yuefu poetry, on par with Zhang Ji, and particularly famous for his palace ci.
马戴: Ma Dai was a Late Tang Dynasty poet, whose main works were poems. He served as Longyang Wei and Taixue Boshi.
元稹: Yuan Zhen was a Mid-Tang Dynasty poet, courtesy name Weizhi, who often exchanged poems with Bai Juyi, and they were known together as "Yuan Bai," representing the "Yuanhe style."
沈佺期: Shen Quanqi was an Early Tang Dynasty poet, especially skilled in seven-character poems, known with Song Zhiwen as "Shen Song," and was one of the founders of regulated verse metrics.
韩愈: Han Yu was an outstanding Mid-Tang Dynasty literary figure and thinker, a proponent of the ancient prose movement, whose poetry style was bold and unrestrained, not shying away from roughness.
杜荀鹤: Du Xunhe, a Late Tang Dynasty poet, courtesy name Yanzhi, sobriquet Jiuhuashanren, rose to the rank of Hanlin Xueshi, and his works were collected as "Tangfeng Ji."
朱庆余: Zhu Qingyu, a Mid-Tang Dynasty poet, courtesy name Kejiu, from Yuezhou, was appreciated by Zhang Ji, passed the imperial examination, and gained fame through his poetry.
许浑: Xu Hun, a Late Tang Dynasty poet, courtesy name Yonghui, from Danyang, served as Cishi. His poetry collection was named after his villa's location, Dingmao Bridge.
李益: Li Yi, a Mid-Tang Dynasty poet, courtesy name Junyu, from Guzang, once served as Mishu Jian. He was skilled in songs and poems, and his works were often sung by musicians in the imperial music bureau.
司空曙: Sikong Shu, a Mid-Tang Dynasty poet, courtesy name Wenming, from Guangping, once served as Shubulangzhong and Yubulangzhong. His poetry style was clear and refined, and he was one of the "Ten Talents of Dali."
刘长卿: Liu Changqing, a Tang Dynasty poet, was skilled in five-character poems and hailed as the "Great Wall of five-character poems." He served as Jiancha Yushi and Suizhou Cishi.
卢纶: Lu Lun was a Tang Dynasty poet, who served as Wenxiang Wei and Jiancha Yushi. His poetry style was elegant, and his works were widely circulated.
崔颢: Cui Hao was a Tang Dynasty poet, who passed the imperial examination during the Kaiyuan era. He was known for his excellent poetic talent, especially for famous pieces like "Huang He Lou."
李颀: Li Qi was a Tang Dynasty poet, who passed the imperial examination during the Kaiyuan era and once served as Xinxiang Wei. His poetic style was unique and has been passed down to this day.
崔涂: Cui Tu was a Tang Dynasty poet, who passed the imperial examination during the Guangqi era, renowned for his poetry, and authored a collection of poems in one volume.
张祜: Zhang Hu, courtesy name Chengji, was a Mid-Tang Dynasty poet, famous for his palace ci.
王涯: Wang Ya, courtesy name Guangjin, was a Mid-Tang Dynasty chancellor and poet, learned and talented, with elegant thoughts in his writings, but was eventually killed due to factional struggles.
张九龄: Zhang Jiuling, courtesy name Zishou, was a High Tang Dynasty chancellor and poet, graceful and upright, and his poetry also enjoyed great renown.
宋之问: Song Zhiwen, courtesy name Yanqing, was a poet from the period of Wu Zetian to Emperor Ruizong of Tang, known for his five-character poems. He once attached himself to powerful officials and was later granted death.
高适: Gao Shi, courtesy name Dafu, was a High Tang Dynasty poet and Jiedushi, who only began writing poetry after fifty years old, and was famous for his frontier poetry and heroic spirit.
钱起: Qian Qi, courtesy name Zhongwen, was a Tang Dynasty poet, known as one of the 'Ten Talents of Dali' alongside Han Hong and Li Duan, with a novel poetic style and clear, elegant reasoning.
元结: Yuan Jie, courtesy name Cishan, was a Tang Dynasty official and poet. He served as the Cishi of Daozhou, benefiting the people, and his poetry often reflected their hardships.
韩翃: Han Hong, courtesy name Junping, was a Tang Dynasty poet and one of the 'Ten Talents of Dali'. His poetry was rich in spirit and highly praised.
韦应物: Wei Yingwu, a Tang Dynasty poet, once served as the Cishi of Suzhou. His poetry was tranquil and simple, earning him the title 'Tao Wei', placing him alongside Tao Yuanming.
岑参: Cen Can, a Tang Dynasty poet, traveled to the frontier many times, and his poetry is known for its clear diction, magnificent style, and frequent depiction of frontier scenery.
严维: Yan Wei was a Tang Dynasty poet, courtesy name Zhengwen, from Shanyin, Yuezhou. He was known for his ornate poetry and served as an editor in the Imperial Library.
吴文英: Wu Wenying was a Southern Song ci poet, courtesy name JunT, pen name Mengchuang. He never held office but composed a large number of ci known for their intricate beauty and profound depth.
晏几道: Yan Jidao was a Northern Song ci poet, courtesy name Shuyuan, pen name Xiaoshan. He was famous for his yuefu ci, and his collection 《Xiaoshan Ci》 is still in existence.
张炎: Zhang Yan was a ci poet of the late Southern Song and early Yuan dynasties, courtesy name Shuxia, pen name Yutian. After the fall of the Song, he refused to serve and was famous for his long and short verses, especially his 'Spring Water ci'.
贺铸: He Zhu was a Northern Song ci poet, courtesy name Fanghui, pen name Qinghu Yilao. He was a master of composing ci, and was known as 'He Meizi' for the line 'when plums turn yellow, it rains'.
刘辰翁: Liu Chenweng (1232—1297), courtesy name Huimeng, pen name Xuxi, was a native of Ji'an, Jiangxi in the late Southern Song Dynasty, famous for his poetry and prose, with his works collected in 《Xuxi Xiansheng Ji》.
周密: Zhou Mi (1232—1298), courtesy name Gongjin, pen name Caocuang, was an important ci poet, historian, and bibliographer of the late Southern Song Dynasty, author of 《Wulin Jiushi》, 《Qidong Yeyu》, and other works.
张元干: Zhang Yuangan (1091—1161), courtesy name Zhongzong, pen name Luchuan Jushi, was a patriotic ci poet of the Southern Song Dynasty, known for his majestic ci style, with his works collected in 《Luchuan Jushi Ci》.
吕渭老: Lu Weilao, courtesy name Shengqiu, from Jiaxing, was a court poet of the late Northern Song Dynasty, and few of his poems have survived.
张先: Zhang Xian (990—1078), courtesy name Ziye, was a Northern Song ci poet, on par with Liu Yong, known for his ci, with his works collected in 《Zhang Duguan Ji》.
史达祖: Shi Dazu was a Southern Song ci poet, courtesy name Bangqing, pen name Meixi, skilled in composing ci, and his collection 《Meixi Ci》 is still in existence.
蔡伸: Cai Shen was a ci poet of the late Northern Song and early Southern Song dynasties, courtesy name Shendao, who held several local official positions.
晁补之: Chao Buzhi was a famous litterateur of the Northern Song Dynasty, courtesy name Wujiu, pen name Guilaizi, and was known as one of the 'Four Scholars of Su's School' alongside Huang Tingjian, with his work 《Jilei Ji》.
蒋捷: Jiang Jie was a Southern Song ci poet, courtesy name Shengyu, pen name Zhushan, who lived in reclusion after the Yuan Dynasty came to power, famous for his ci, with his collection 《Zhushan Ci》.
周紫芝: Zhou Zizhi was a Southern Song poet and ci poet, courtesy name Shaoyin, pen name Zhupo Jushi, author of 《Taicang Timi Ji》 and 《Zhupo Shihua》.
张孝祥: Zhang Xiaoxiang (1132-1170) was a famous ci poet and patriotic official of the Southern Song Dynasty, known for his bold and unrestrained poetic style.
袁去华: Yuan Quhua was a successful candidate in the imperial examination during the Shaoxing era of the Southern Song Dynasty; his ci works are still extant today, and he authored 'Shizhai Leigao' and 'Yuan Xuanqing Ci'.
刘克庄: Liu Kezhuang (1187-1269) was a famous literati and historian of the Southern Song Dynasty, skilled in both poetry and prose, and was known as 'Mr. Houcun'.
卢祖皋: Lu Zugao was a native of Yongjia in the Southern Song Dynasty, a successful candidate in the imperial examination in the fifth year of Qingyuan (1199), and his ci work 'Pujiang Ci' is still extant.
祖咏: Zu Yong was a Tang Dynasty poet from Luoyang, a successful candidate in the imperial examination during the Kaiyuan era, befriended Wang Wei, and is known for a collection of his poems.
李之仪: Li Zhiyi was a literati of the Northern Song Dynasty, a successful candidate in the imperial examination during Emperor Shenzong's Xining reign, known for his ci and poetry, and authored 'Guxi Jushi Qianhou Ji'.
范成大: Fan Chengda was a famous literati and poet during the Southern Song Dynasty (1126-1193), known for his outstanding achievements in poetry.
韩元吉: Han Yuanji (1118-c. 1186) was a minister and scholar of the Southern Song Dynasty, serving as Minister of Personnel, and was renowned for his literary talent.
王沂孙: Wang Yisun was a ci poet from the late Southern Song to the early Yuan Dynasty, famous for his creation of heroic and unrestrained ci, with 'Bishan Yuefu' being passed down.
刘方平: Liu Fangping was a native of Henan in the Tang Dynasty; he was good friends with Yuan Dexiu but unwilling to serve as an official, and a collection of his poems is still extant.
仲殊: Zhong Shu was a Buddhist monk of the Northern Song Dynasty, originally named Zhang Hui, skilled in poetry and ci composition, with a brilliant and elegant ci style, and once associated with Su Shi.
刘过: Liu Guo was a Southern Song poet and anti-Jin patriot, with the courtesy name Gaizhi and the sobriquet Longzhou Daoren; he never held office in his life, and his poems are bold and unrestrained, engaging in poetic exchanges with poets like Lu You.
叶梦得: Ye Mengde was an official and literati from the late Northern Song to the early Southern Song Dynasty, with the courtesy name Shaoyun and the sobriquet Shilin Jushi, known for his numerous writings and excellent poetry and prose.
刘一止: Liu Yizhi was a Southern Song official and poet, with the courtesy name Xingjian; he was repeatedly dismissed from office for his outspoken advice, and his poetry and prose are collected in 'Tiaoxi Ji'.
万俟咏: Wanqiu Yong was a ci poet of the late Northern Song Dynasty, with the courtesy name Yayan and the sobriquet Daliang Ciyin; he was skilled in composing new melodies, and his ci style emulated Liu Yong.
丘为: Qiu Wei was a Tang Dynasty poet, who lived to be ninety-six years old, was friends with Wang Wei and Liu Changqing, and his poems are still extant.
刘眘虚: Liu Shenxu was a poet during the Tianbao era of the Tang Dynasty, who once served as the county magistrate of Xiaxian, and one volume of his works is extant.
严仁: Yan Ren was a native of Shaowu in the Song Dynasty, with the sobriquet Qiaoxi, and was known as one of the 'Three Yans of Shaowu' along with Yan Yu and Yan Can; most of his poems have been lost.
彭元逊: Peng Yuanxun, whose birth and death dates are unknown, was a ci poet of the Song Dynasty; his works are scattered throughout 'Quan Song Ci', and he was known for his graceful and subtle style.
陈克: Chen Ke was a native of Linhai in the Song Dynasty, with the courtesy name Zigao and the sobriquet Chicheng Jushi; he once served as an official for compiling imperial edicts, and a collection of his poetry and prose is extant.
王安石: Wang Anshi was a famous politician, thinker, and writer of the Northern Song Dynasty, who implemented far-reaching reforms.
陈与义: Chen Yuyi was a poet of the early Southern Song Dynasty, renowned for his poetry which often reflected the displacement of war and patriotic sentiments.
俞国宝: Yu Guobao was a Grand Student during the Chunxi era of Emperor Xiaozong's reign in the Southern Song Dynasty, who gained official appointment after his ci inscription on a white screen in a West Lake tavern was admired by Emperor Gaozong.
